But even Kuyt would have been the first to recognise the helping hand Fenerbahce were afforded. Liverpool were meek, naïve, and while the Turkish side danced in the rain on the Asian side of the city, Iraola was left to dissect the most chastening 90 minutes of his short Anfield career.

“It’s frustration because it’s a difficult place to come here and to play,” said Iraola. “During most of the game, we were thinking: ‘OK we can win this one.’ But obviously it hasn’t happened. We conceded, I think, messy goals, especially the first and the third one. The second one is a rebound.”

Yet it all started so smoothly. For all that Fenerbahce tried to put Liverpool out of their stride with a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling, Iraola’s side kept the ball well and they might have been ahead in the fifth minute but Victor Muñoz and Bradley Barcola, playing as a central striker, erred.

Another chance went begging when Joe Gomez fizzed a ball across the six-yard box that was screaming to be converted, but nobody could apply the finishing touch. When Trey Nyoni put Liverpool ahead, it seemed like all those local predictions of a resounding away win would come true.

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

#1000. Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

#998. Meet the world's most famous pub team: How a Sex Pistol, Superman and Vinnie Jones took Hollywood United  beyond Sunset Boulevard via private jet - and even rubbed shoulders with David Beckham's LA Galaxy

Published: 09:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:29 EST, 24 November 2026

They had a World Cup winner in defence, Superman in their squad and a Sex Pistol in charge of recruitment.

There's a clue in the name, but Hollywood United must have been the wildest, most star-studded pub football team of all time.

Ray Winstone, Jason Statham, Mike Myers and Vinnie Jones all turned out for a team that grew out of a gathering of British expats at the Cat & Fiddle pub in the late Eighties.

It being Hollywood, they travelled to matches by private jet and they even took on David Beckham in a charity match.

Now, as the Sex Pistols prepare to embark on a tour marking the 50th anniversary of their debut single, guitarist Steve Jones has revealed how he assembled the extraordinary side on Hollywood's Sunset Boulevard.

Among those who pulled on the shirt were France's World Cup-winning defender Frank Leboeuf, former Scotland captain Richard Gough and Brandon Routh, the American actor who played the superhero in the 2006 film Superman Returns.

Routh was given no special treatment by his team-mates, who would mockingly shout ‘Superman!’ whenever he made a mistake.

Hollywood United is the world's most famous pub team - featuring a littany of high-profile stars

Created by British expat and Sex Pistols star Steve Jones (right), United have rubbed shoulders with the likes of David Beckham

Vinnie Jones, meanwhile, had apparently lost none of the competitive instincts that characterised his career in English football.

In 2002, it was reported that he had been sent off just 15 seconds after coming on as a substitute in a Hollywood United friendly.

Anthony LaPaglia, the Australian actor who starred in the hit television series Without a Trace, was their goalkeeper.

There were members of the Sex Pistols, The Cult and Def Leppard, as well as actors such as Ralf Little.

But there were also rather less celebrated footballers.

‘The start of it was with me and Anthony LaPaglia; he was a goalie, and from there it turned into Hollywood United,’ Jones told the Telegraph.

‘We always used to play in a league with a bunch of regular blokes, carpenters and so on, then we got a few more faces who wanted to start kicking about with us like Vinnie Jones.’

The two Joneses met in a video shop in Los Angeles and the former Wimbledon hardman, who had embarked on a film career with Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, needed little persuasion to join.

‘He was up for a laugh, and he knows where to put a ball. Most of the team were amateurs, but we were decent and reached a certain level.’

In November 2007, Hollywood United took on Beckham's LA Galaxy in a charity match.

England manager Steve McClaren had flown to California to assess Beckham's fitness ahead of a European Championship qualifier against Croatia. It's not clear whether he attended the match, which Hollywood United lost 12-4. Beckham scored twice, as did Leboeuf and over 5,000 spectators raised more than $100,000 for victims of the California wildfires.

Steve Jones, now 71, had himself broken one of football's golden rules by changing his allegiance.

Vinnie Jones (left) and Ray Winstone (right) have turned out for the amateur football team

Actor Anthony LaPaglia lets the team travel on his private jet to matches across America

Having followed QPR as a schoolboy in west London and also been associated with Fulham, he became a Chelsea supporter after moving to California and getting sober.

Chelsea's games were available on American television and his lifelong friend and fellow Sex Pistol Paul Cook was already a diehard Blues fan.

Hollywood United played at Griffith Park, beneath the famous Hollywood sign, but their adventures would take them considerably further afield.

LaPaglia would arrange private jets to transport the players to matches.

Gough recalls one trip when the team flew to Vancouver for a charity match before heading straight to the Mexican resort of Puerto Vallarta to play a side of former Mexico internationals.

Vinnie Jones also told the Guardian in 2007 that Hollywood United had fielded nine former international footballers in a single match.

The club's ranks included former Liverpool and Newcastle defender Barry Venison and United States internationals Alexi Lalas and Eric Wynalda.

Winstone, a lifelong West Ham fan, found playing in the Californian heat rather more demanding than he had anticipated.

He later recalled being so exhausted by the time the ball reached him that he was barely able to kick it. And he wasn't particularly impressed by the willingness of former Chelsea defender Leboeuf to pass the ball, describing the Frenchman as a greedy player.

Among those watching from the touchline was the actor John Hurt, who was in town filming Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull with Winstone.

Some of the rock stars had impressive footballing pedigrees.

Ian Astbury, the lead singer of The Cult, had played boys' club football in Glasgow alongside future Everton and Scotland striker Graeme Sharp.

Gough, meanwhile, struck up a conversation with a team-mate from Northern Ireland without having the slightest idea he was Vivian Campbell, the guitarist of Def Leppard.

Sex Pistol Jones, who has lived in Los Angeles for more than 40 years, is returning to Britain next month for a tour marking the 50th anniversary of the release of Anarchy in the UK.

He still regularly attends football matches whenever he is back in England, although he has little time for the corporate hospitality enjoyed by many of his celebrity contemporaries.

‘I don't care where I sit, but I'm not interested in sitting in some box with a bunch of t***ers.’

Ezri Konsa booked after Ayaosi gets to a loose ball first near the touchline. Moments before that, White and Raya messed about with the ball and there were some choice words from Rice and Arteta. Arsenal have dropped their standards so far in the half.

Arteta is really raging on the touchline. He is not happy with how Arsenal have started this second half. He just aimed a few verbals at White for a defensive mix-up. White had actually already received an apology from Raya and didn’t seem to think it was his fault.

Rice with a chance to pick out Madueke on the counter but his diagonal pass was cut out. Slavia have been sent out with a flea in their ear, and have been much improved so far. Arteta will want Arsenal to stay serious and weather this spell.

Tonight has been a reminder of how good Martin Zubimendi is in the air. He’s wearing a face mask because of a broken nose but he’s won every header he has gone for. He’s not particularly tall but he has a great leap and timing.

Slavia Prague have a free-kick on the edge of Arsenal’s box after Konsa goes sliding in. Much more like it from Slavia Prague early on, Arsenal a little dozy since the restart.

Kubiak shoots low from the free-kick, but it is straight into the wall.

The home crowd have something to shout about for the first time tonight. Kubiak brings a decent save out of David Raya after shooting with his left foot from 25 yards. Then Raya slices a kick out for a throw-in.

Slavia have made a double sub: Suleiman and Sturm off, N’Guessan and Chytil on.

From the early stages of the game, the home team have tried to sprint up to the ball and pressure Arsenal, but they have been manipulated and played through so easily at times. When they do lock on man-to-man, Arsenal are hitting Madueke, Eze and Gyokeres early who are pinning defenders and then laying the ball off to runners.

Arsenal are dispatching another Champions League league phase opponent with ease, but the big positive has been the performances of Eze, Gyokeres and Madueke. Without Saka, Arteta needs them to step up and provide goals and assists. Albeit against poor opposition, they have all looked dangerous. Might we see half-time changes with Saturday’s game against Hull in mind?

Kubiak down and there are loud appeals for a Slavia free-kick but the referee was not having any of it. Gyokeres proves an otlet again, but his pass towards Madueke was too strong.

Arsenal have a corner and they are rampant. Eze with a flick around the corner which almost finds Gyokeres, they are playing with plenty of attacking panache. The quality of opposition needs accounting for but Arteta will be delighted given he made six changes.

Gabriel then threatens after Domchak spills Madueke’s cross, but his effort was blocked.

Arsenal wasted a counter initially with Eze running into a Zubimendi pass but they kept it alive and eventually punished their hosts. Merino with a cute pass back into Gyokeres’s path, and he took his time before curling a shot in off the far post. Arsenal should not be caught from here.

If you thought the Gyokeres assist was good, then that goal was even better. Gorgeous finish. That takes him to three assists and two goals in his past five games.

What a finish from Viktor Gyökeres from a tight angle 📐🎯 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/EET5P7aJ2X

Slavia Prague have had their first shot: Holes poking wide after a long throw was hurled into the box. Not much more than a half chance.

The referee is now having a word with Rice after he complained about Eze not being awarded a free-kick. Slavia have settled down a touch after that very rocky period, but they are still to muster a shot on goal.

Declan Rice is throwing a blanket over any flickering embers of a Slavia Prague attack, and then he is running the game from there. Arsenal’s captain on the night has been imperious so far.

Now Declan Rice feeds the ball straight through the six-yard box but Hincapie could not quite make it his to score a tap-in. Surely a question of when not if Arsenal put this game to bed.

Eze and Madueke are feeling it tonight. Slavia’s full-backs have been going through footballing hell in this opening half an hour.

Eze and Hincapie’s turn to cause problems down the left, the left-back’s pull-back evaded everyone, before Eze sat down the defender in the box but his shot was blocked.

Then Domchak saves from point-blank range to deny Merino! Slick play between Madueke and White to carve out the chance.

Arsenal really should have buried the second.

Domchak claimed Rice’s cross from the free-kick and Slavia Prague tried to counter-attack, but it was really diligent defensive work from Madueke to snuff out the danger. Arsenal continue to look in complete control.

Madueke then proves a thorn in the Slavia defence’s side, sitting down the left-back and standing up a cross to the back post. Gyokeres won the header, then Merino glanced over.

A moment of promise from Slavia Prague, but their pull-back to the edge of the box is picked up by Arsenal and Eze skips through a couple of challenges before being brought down by Moses. Yellow card for the Slavia Prague midfielder.

Then Ayaosi concedes a cheap free-kick against Hincapie, in a crossing position wide left.

Arsenal leaving themselves light at the back, but White, Gabriel and Konsa are happy dealing with the one-on-one duels, they look physically stronger than the Slavia forwards. Madueke, aside from his goal, has been very tidy on the ball so far.

Sharp interplay from Gyokeres and Eze again, teeing up Merino to sting the palms of the goalkeeper with a shot from the edge of the box. Arsenal corner.

Last time out in the Champions League against Lille, Arsenal’s squad players in attack failed to seize their chance but this has been much more promising from them.

Domchak makes a scrambling save on the line to stop Arsenal going two up, and possibly killing the game. Zubimendi’s break forward created the danger, and Gyokeres and Hincapie were close to applying the finish.

There was a moment just after scoring where Hincapie was caught forward on the overlap, and who else but Declan Rice was on hand to mop up the counter-attack in the left-back zone? Order restored, and Arsenal back on top in the game soon after.

Slavia Prague make a mess of a simple long ball forward, disobeying the old maxim that says never let the ball bounce. Gyokeres was alive though, hooking the ball behind the defence with a clever early pass. Madueke’s pace was always going to send him clear, and he slipped the ball through the legs of the goalkeeper Domchak.

That didn’t take long. Arsenal have dominated the ball in these opening exchanges and now they have scored with their first real chance. It’s a lovely pass by Gyokeres, who is not known for his intricate build-up play, and Madueke’s pace gets him behind. Madueke’s third goal of the season.

A fantastic pass from Gyökeres and a lovely finish from Madueke 🪄 The Arsenal attackers combine to great effect 🤝 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/blmMILZxok

With Merino, Zubimendi and Rice in Arsenal’s midfield, there is perhaps no natural creator, but the three of them are rotating, taking it in turns to stand between the centre-backs or go high.

Madueke stands up a cross which Slavia Prague head clear. Most of the game is being played in the home team’s half, which you would expect. Arsenal probing and moving the ball patiently.

Madueke and Ben White then combine well, but Eze cannot quite let fly from a central position. The Arsenal left-winger drifting across the line to receive the ball in that move.

Quite an industrious start from the home team, trying to close Arsenal down, but Merino and Zubimendi combined well in a tight space to help Arsenal move forward. The flag goes up against Ben White for offside, possibly mistakenly.

At the other end Sturm caused Konsa a problem, but the Arsenal defender recovered well and the goal kick decision was in his favour too, much to the annoyance of the home crowd.

Arsenal also paid their respects at Colney to the 30-year-old Spanish player who died after a collision with the Andorra’s goalkeeper.

Declan Rice is wearing the captain’s armband and leads Arsenal out at a smoky Fortuna Arena. Slavia Prague are celebrating their 144th birthday, and marked the occasion with a choir and classical music.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel)

William Saliba is BACK 💥 https://t.co/aRmJoIlxSc

Liverpool twice threw away a lead to lose against Fenerbahce in Istanbul. That has some relevance to Arsenal because Liverpool are one of the teams above them in the league phase table. Win in Prague, and they will move one point clear of their Premier League rivals.

Real Madrid struck late to drag themselves out of jail at AEK Athens and join PSG on maximum points from four games. Arsenal cannot catch those two sides tonight, but they do host Real next month.

Slavia are without their top scorer from the last two seasons, Tomas Chory, for rather unusual reasons. He has been banished from the club following a series of misdemeanours, the latest of which was showing the middle finger to the referee in a recent league game. Slavia have made it clear he won’t be playing for the club again, despite his importance to the team over the past few years.

Chory was also sent off for Czech Republic against Turkey at Euro 2024.

😬 Pandemonium after the final whistle! Czech Republic's Tomáš Chorý is shown a red card, with multiple others yellow carded, as players and staff from both sides clash 🟥 #Euro2024 | #CZETUR https://t.co/5xhR0Bwafa

Without meaning to be rude, I think it’s fair to say Slavia are not the most formidable opponent that Arsenal will face this season.

They are on a 22-game winless streak in the Champions League, dating back to 2007. If they don’t win tonight, they will equal the longest winless run in European Cup/Champions League history, shared with AEK Athens (1989-2006) and Steau Bucharest (2006-2013).

Slavia Prague XI: Domchak, Holes, Zima, Vlcek, Suleiman, Moses, Sadilek, Kubiak, Ayaosi, Sturm, Nowak

Subs: Markovic, Rezek, Chaloupek, N’Guessan, Chytil, Provod, Diakite, Kacor, Jurasek, Konecny, Barcot, Kotrba

Good evening from a chilly Prague, where Arsenal are looking for a repeat of the 3-0 victory they secured here exactly one year ago. It’s a remarkable coincidence that Mikel Arteta’s team have travelled to face Slavia Prague on November 4th in back-to-back years.

On that occasion last year, Max Dowman became the youngest player in Champions League history. He should get more minutes tonight from the bench, given that he is currently suspended from Premier League action following his controversial red card against Fleetwood last week.

That’s the most Arteta has rotated between a Premier League and Champions League game so far this season. Telling perhaps that Konsa, Gabriel and Rice – the team’s defensive bedrock – stay in place. But changes on both sides at full-back, and in the attacking midfield areas.

Arsenal XI: Raya; White, Konsa, Gabriel, Hincapie; Rice, Zubimendi, Merino; Madueke, Gyokeres, Eze

Subs: Kepa, Meslier, Saliba, Mosquera, Timber, Calafiori, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard, Guimaraes, Tzolis, Dowman, Havertz

🔵 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🟡 Six changes for our Champions League test 👊

Arsenal’s critics will still grumble about the style of victory, but, of all clubs, this is a team who have no obligation to play in a way that neutrals might enjoy. Arsenal spent so much of Arsene Wenger’s 22-year reign playing football that was mostly stylish but only sometimes effective in big games. Now they are mostly effective but only occasionally stylish on such occasions. If you asked all the travelling fans at Anfield which they prefer, you would receive an overwhelming response.

David Raya has kept a clean sheet in 54% of his Champions League starts (21 clean sheets from 39 starts), the best ratio of any goalkeeper to start at least 25 games in the competition. 🤯🇪🇸 https://t.co/A1Zpn8kJN9

Arsenal return to Slavia Prague for the third time under Mikel Arteta knowing that three points will be another step towards a top-eight finish in the Champions League league phase.

Arteta’s team were 4-0 winners in the Czech capital in a 2021 Europa League quarter-final second leg, and 3-0 victors at this stage of the Champions League a year ago. Bukayo Saka opened the scoring with a penalty before two second-half goals from Mikel Merino.

Paris-St Germain are top of the table on 12 points after their rout against Villarreal last night. Real Madrid, Liverpool and Real Betis are the three teams who have the chance to join them on maximum points. Arsenal will jump to 10 points with a win, above Bayern Munich, Sporting and Aston Villa at a minimum.

Slavia Prague are top of the Czech league and unbeaten after 13 games this season, but they are winless in the Champions League after fixtures against Lens, Sabah and Fernerbahce.

The fixture should be a presentable opportunity for Arteta to rotate his team, especially after a physically taxing game at Anfield where Arsenal showed their mettle to win at Liverpool’s home for the first time since 2012.

Arsenal’s second-string is very strong, though they did not cover themselves in glory at Fleetwood in the League Cup last week when Max Dowman was sent off. Given the 16-year-old is banned for another two Premier League games, and the attention Arteta’s touchline reaction to the red card attracted, one wonders if he might want to seize a chance to put Dowman back on the horse.

William Saliba’s return to full training is very welcome news, despite Ezri Konsa impressing in his absence. Saliba travelled with the squad to Prague, and could make his first appearance of the season following a back injury which flared up in France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain. With fixtures against Manchester City, Borussia Dortmund, Brentford, Spurs, Real Madrid, Bournemouth and Manchester United before the end of 2026 though, they will not want rush him.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

#996. How to make climate anxiety your superpower

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Download the Nature Podcast 23 November 2026

Late last week the UN’s climate conference, COP31, failed to reach a consensus on its headline message. That news came on the heels of the UN acknowledging that the 1.5 ˚C warming limit set out in Paris will be breached. So, it’s easy to feel anxious in a world where it seems that not enough is being done about climate change. But is it possible to overcome such anxiety or even use it?

In the final episode of Cooked? I open up about my own climate anxiety and discover that there are still things that I can do to battle climate change. And how those small individual actions could potentially lead to more systemic change.

00:00 Can I do anything about my climate anxiety?

04:43 What the science says about ‘ecoanxiety’

11:35 Can individuals really do anything?

Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’

The rise of eco-anxiety: scientists wake up to the mental-health toll of climate change

This episode was written and produced by Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was the editor. Music was by Akio Jefferson, Jonathan Maiocco, Aerial Circles, and Lionel Cohen, and was provided by Triple Scoop Music via Getty Images. Thanks to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu and Elizabeth Howe for featuring in this episode.

Nick Petrić Howe: Hi mum, can you hear me okay?

Nick Petrić Howe: If you’ve been listening to this series, you’ll know that I’ve been struggling a bit with anxiety about the climate. If you’re just joining us now, hi, I’m Nick Petrić Howe and I have a climate anxiety problem. Throughout this series, I’ve spoken to a lot of scientists about the big ideas and big data that we can use to tackle climate change, but I haven’t really addressed the core reason of why I wanted to do this — to figure out what to do with my own feelings about climate change.

I wanted to know if I’d always felt this way, and if so, what I could do about it. So, I called up an expert on me. My mum.

Nick Petrić Howe: Can I record this call for work?

Elizabeth Howe: Yeah, course you can yeah

Nick Petrić Howe: This wasn’t exactly what I was expecting. I feel like I worry about things and have worried about them a lot throughout my life. It’s why I decided to study biology when I finished school, eventually doing a PhD — to figure out if there was some way to help save the planet. So, I tried a different tack.

Nick Petrić Howe: Do you ever remember me worrying about, like, the environment and stuff. Elizabeth Howe: Oh God yeah. You were always thinking about stuff like that.

Elizabeth Howe: Well because you said— there was a big thing about climate change and you said ‘oh well climate change isn’t real because, you see, what happens is, in science, is that the world has these ice ages and then everything melts and then daa daa daa daaa.’ So you said, ‘it’s just a normal event, it’s not anything to do with global warming and it’s a load of rubbish.’ But you were always looking into stuff like that and listening to stuff like that. You were very interested in the scientific explanations for things.

Nick Petrić Howe: I’m not sure how I feel about that to be honest.

Nick Petrić Howe: Not gonna lie, being outed as a junior climate denier was not on my bingo card for this year. We eventually came to the conclusion that this was a phase I went through when I was quite young and hadn’t quite understood that people could just well… lie on national television. Misinformation, unfortunately, isn’t just a new thing. When I was a kid in the 90s, there were campaigns to make climate research seem a lot more questionable than now, and established politicians like Lord Nigel Lawson in the UK openly criticised the science.

At least, it seemed, I was interested in the climate. For the record, now I absolutely am convinced, along with the scientific community, that climate change is real and human caused.

And, even according to my mum, as I got older, I cared more about the climate, even if I wasn’t necessarily worried.

Elizabeth Howe: I don’t think you were particularly too worried…

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, I remember thinking when I was a teenager and I was more appraised of the actual facts, that climate change was a solvable problem. One that my generation could fix. I was filled with notions of all the things that science had accomplished — the moon landings, the internet, and general relativity — breakthroughs that solved problems once thought insurmountable. It took me getting older to become a bit more jaded, concerned that we’d not done enough soon enough and that maybe it was too late.

But this got me thinking, if I wasn’t worried once and even felt hopeful. Is that something I could recapture? This series has already taught me that in many ways we’ve done more than I thought to tackle climate change and that people are actively working on solutions. But that only goes so far to assuage my own anxiety. So you’ll forgive me if I spend this episode figuring out if there’s something that can help me. Is there anything I can do?

Nick Petrić Howe: As I said, I’ve struggled with anxiety about climate change. Sometimes I feel paralysed by how hopeless it all seems. There’s so much to do and it’s not getting done fast enough. At the same time, every other week there seems to be another climate record smashed or a natural disaster exacerbated by climate change.

It’s easy to feel anxious. So, in this third and final episode of Cooked? I wanted to know - am I normal? Or am I bit of an outlier here? Are other people having these feelings of hopelessness in the face of climate change.

So, I called up one of the world experts on how climate change is affecting mental health.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Emma Lawrance, from Imperial College London. After figuring out our settings, we connected on a slightly better line. And Emma told me that I’m by no means alone, in fact, it turns out there is a name for what I’m feeling. There’s a few actually.

Emma Lawrance: So there is this kind of emerging plethora of terms really that all centre on this kind of umbrella of what we might call psychological responses or emotional responses to the climate crisis. And so some of those terms can be things like climate related distress, climate anxiety, eco anxiety, ecological grief, solastalgia.

Nick Petrić Howe: And while there are differences between these terms, for the purposes of the podcast I’m just going to say eco-anxiety — the anxiety about climate change and environmental destruction, as that seems the most fitting with my experience.

And one of the first things that Emma impressed upon me is that there’s a lot we don’t know about eco-anxiety. This is a rapidly emerging field, but eco-anxiety is a thing that a lot of people are feeling. Especially if they’re dealing with the consequences of climate change.

Emma Lawrance: So for instance, in our sample of nearly 3,000 young people surveyed across the US, one fifth of the young people who didn't report experiencing a climate change-related event were afraid to have children that rose to one third of the young people who said they had already experienced a climate change-related event. And there was a correlation between the people sort of self-reporting and looking at their postcodes and where you know, climate hazards had been in the US. So, they seem to be kind of reflecting sort of a real-world experience.

Nick Petrić Howe: And that makes sense. If climate change is affecting you, then you would worry about it. I know my own anxiety spiked during the heatwaves, wildfires and droughts of this last British summer. But that does also mean that there are certain people who worry a bit more than others.

Emma Lawrance: There's more and more studies showing that eco-anxiety is definitely not like a white Western phenomenon. This experience of distress and what can be called eco-anxiety in response to changing climate is actually much higher in the countries and in the communities where these impacts are already occurring.

Nick Petrić Howe: That might surprise you, it certainly did me - In some ways, I had thought that maybe this was a worry more for people like me. Western, relatively well-off folks, who have time to worry about things. But, if my anxiety spiked over one record breaking summer, perhaps it shouldn’t be shocking that people facing these impacts week after week in the developing countries most effected, but least responsible for climate change are worried too. And they’re only getting more worried.

Emma Lawrance: It's happening in ways that are then compounding. So people are experiencing not just one, but multiple kind of stresses and disasters, often coming back-to-back and they're not having time to recover before the next one hits that experience into place with this awareness of, well, what's to come? The awareness of the injustice of the situation of often kind of insufficient climate action and power dynamics between, you know, the people who are affected and the people causing the problem and growing inequalities in some spaces or many spaces globally. those things are we're seeing this really rapid increase in the use of the term eco anxiety. So I think there's over a 4,000-fold percent increase in Google searches. five-year period. And so, it’s really skyrocketed

Nick Petrić Howe: Strangely, it feels a little better to know that I’m not alone in these feelings. Perhaps I am a bit more normal than I thought. But I wanted to know what could be done about these feelings. For me, the anxiety has sometimes been paralysing. I haven’t wanted to engage with climate news, which, as I’ve said, is a bit of a funny position to be in as a science journalist. And Emma explained to me that, for some people it can be like that. It can even affect people’s daily lives, and those people may need some extra help and support, but for many people this anxiety can be quite an understandable reaction.

Emma Lawrance: Eco-anxiety isn't something that the vast majority of researchers and people living with these experiences and profession and, mental health professionals would say needs to be a quote unquote, like diagnosis. And it's something that is, can be very rational. It's understandable, and often proportionate to feel alarm, to feel distressed, to feel the strong emotions in response to the facts of the climate crisis.

Nick Petrić Howe: And for some people, it may even be a feeling they want to hold onto. They can use it to push them to battle climate change.

Emma Lawrance: We also know that people who are feeling that distress are more likely to be taking pro-environmental action. We know that collective action, particularly rather than individual action can help you like hold high distress and protect your mental health and wellbeing. it's not sometimes holding distress can impact, you know, is related to poorer mental health, it's related to higher insomnia, et cetera. But young people are saying, you know, we don't want our distress to be taken away in a sense, because this shows that we care. It shows that we care about the world. It can be fuel for action, but that action needs to be often done with others. And also can for some people lead into action that ends up providing more meaning and joy and purpose and it can be a really good thing, but for others it can be overwhelming and paralysing and have really severe impacts on their life

Nick Petrić Howe: So, to my question of what I’m supposed to do with these feelings... I think I’m already doing it. These feelings can overwhelm, and I’ve certainly felt that. But maybe doing something is a way to help live with these anxious feelings. The question is though, what do you do?

Kimberly Nicholas: I really think if your listeners were taking these high-impact climate actions just 20 minutes a day. It would be enough.

Nick Petrić Howe: Now, what I don't want to do is make you feel as though the weight of the world is on your shoulders. Saying that you are ultimately responsible for climate change is too much of a burden for any one person to bear. As someone who worries a lot, I think that weight would crush me, frankly. It’s also fair to say that many of these problems are systemic too. Governments, nations, and businesses should all meet ambitious climate targets if we’re to avoid the worst consequences of climate change. And if you live in the US, say, even if you have very minimal emissions compared to your neighbours, you’re likely to have higher emissions than someone in Bangladesh — just because of how baked in carbon emissions are. If you have an electric car in the US, for example, it’s getting electricity from more fossil fuel power plants than someone in Norway. So, it’s easy to think that any individual action is a waste of time.

Kimberly Nicholas: Well, ineffective individual actions are a waste of time.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Kimberly Nicholas, a climate scientist at Lund University. And she’s someone who’s spent quite a bit of time thinking about what individuals can do, and perhaps what they shouldn’t do.

Kimberly Nicholas: We don't need to focus on recycling or canvas bags. People really have the wrong ideas about what individual action means. And so that I think is a myth that we need to dispel. So, it's not about doing everything, it's not that every little thing matters, it's that focusing our limited time and energy where it can really make a difference can lead us to take powerful actions today that do lead to system change.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it’s not just the what that Kimberly has been thinking about, it’s the who too.

Kimberly Nicholas: I really focus on this group that is in the top 10% globally, many of whom are surprised to learn that they are in that group. So if you earn over about 38,000 US dollars or 35,000 euros a year, your income is in the top 10% globally. And that group produces about half of household carbon pollution and also has enormous political, economic, cultural power.

Nick Petrić Howe: I was among those surprised to find myself in that group. Being in the 10% of income doesn’t quite gel with my, admittedly comfortable, but fairly ordinary life. It’s worth saying as well, that power and carbon emissions track income as it rises too. With around a fifth of warming between 1990 and 2020 attributable to people in the top 1% of income, and a bit under a tenth to those in the top 0.1%.

But the top 10%, which I’m going to guess includes a lot of you listening, still have a lot that they can do, according to Kimberly. She notes that things like reducing air travel, investing in low-emission funds, and switching to renewable energy providers could be effective. She’s even created a guide for people online where you can find what the highest impact climate actions you personally can take. She calls it finding your superpower.

Now, there are researchers who are critical of these ideas. Arguing that individual actions, like these, are a distraction from larger more systemic changes that should be taking place. And others have argued that the fossil fuel industry has used individual actions to take onus off themselves. In fact, carbon footprints — which focus on the emissions of an individual — were popularised by the fossil fuel industry.

But I spoke to a lot of different experts for this series, and they mostly agreed on both being important. We’ll need individual actions and systemic changes. And one doesn’t preclude the other. Things like individual actions may also actually lead to bigger changes.

This is also why Kimberly focuses on specific actions that she feels will have the biggest impacts. And one key one for those who live in a liberal democracy, where you can freely vote for your leaders, is to try and use your individual power to lead to systemic change.

Kimberly Nicholas: For those of us who do live in those countries, we have incredible powers like voting and encouraging and getting others to vote, mobilizing voting, joining a political party or organization that's taking powerful climate action. And the reason those types of actions are so important is that climate policies that affect everyone in a society, of course, have enormous potential, far bigger than, you know, our everyday lives at home, to really move the needle and dramatically decrease climate pollution.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it’s not just politics. This could also be things like engaging with climate action at work. Many workplaces have climate goals and there are usually other keen people you can connect with to try and make these goals happen. Maybe your own climate efforts are small, but a company of 10, 100 or thousands of people could make a much more tangible difference.

For example, there has been an employee-led effort to urge their companies to leave the US Chamber of Commerce. This business association rejected the scientific consensus on climate change until 2019 and has historically obstructed climate action. More recently, it has acknowledged that humans contribute to climate change, however, it still lobbied against the Inflation Reduction Act. So, climate concerned employees of the companies that are members of the Chamber have been petitioning their firms to leave the organisation. Many of those companies have now objected to the Chamber’s climate policies.

In fact, when I spoke to Kimberly it seemed that a lot of the ‘individual’ actions she suggested were really about connecting to others, be that political organising or simply socialising with other climate-conscious people. Those actions could build to something more, but they could also help with the reason I started this podcast in the first place. Anxiety.

Kimberly Nicholas: We want to make climate action fun. It should be something we look forward to and enjoy doing. That's one of the best parts of our week. and we know that from research, doing things together in community helps prevent burnout, it can help reduce anxiety, it can help motivate us and keep us going. And we all have ups and downs. I mean, we've all had moments of despair working on the climate crisis is not an easy thing to do. but we've also had moments of incredible elation and connection and creativity and joy. So being able to be in community is really powerful.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it could be that by connecting people together, that could ultimately lead to societal change.

Madalina Vlasceanu: I think there's this positive feedback loop by which all of our individual level actions can lead to bigger collective actions. And then collective actions can then trigger system level changes. The system level changes can then make it easier for individuals to take additional individual level actions because they would ideally remove the barriers to action.

Nick Petrić Howe: I have to admit that after my chat with Kimberley, I certainly felt a bit more empowered, but I was still a bit sceptical about the power of individuals. It’s not that I think individuals can’t do anything, it’s just the scale of the challenge that makes me hesitate. Even if I am, or even everyone listening is, the most climate conscious warriors in the world, it probably wouldn’t be enough. Like Kimberley alluded to, those individuals actions need to build towards the systemic. We need to change society.

I was curious about what the research said about the connection between the individual and the systemic and importantly, how can we actually get these small actions to help battle the global problem of climate change. So, I called up Madalina Vlasceanu, a social scientist who’s thought a lot about this exact issue.

Madalina Vlasceanu: So in my work we think about what are some ways in which collective action can be triggered at the individual level and then spread and catalyzed around groups and then collectives and then eventually making some system level pro changes.

Nick Petrić Howe: In our chat, one of the things that Madalina impressed upon me is that, while she believes that individual actions can lead to collective ones and then to systemic change, there are barriers that we need to acknowledge. For example, if you think the transition to renewable energy, the big barrier there is that fossil fuels are hugely subsidised. According to the International Monetary Fund, in 2024 fossil fuel subsidies were around $725 billion worldwide. If the underpricing of environmental costs are taken into account, such as air pollution and their contribution to climate change, that number rises to $6.7 trillion. In either case, fossil fuels are being made cheaper than they should be, which is not ideal when we should be using less of them.

Madalina Vlasceanu: So, our energy system needs to change and this can only happen through laws, policies, regulations that reduce, for example, fossil fuel subsidies currently valued at trillions of dollars. And in order for this to happen, for these systemic regulations to be introduced and enforced, there needs to, of course, be massive awareness campaigns from the public. So the public can push in this direction and make this direction the normative direction. So there is a big component here of the transition that has to do with laws, but the laws will likely change as an effect of pressure from the public.

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, one reason that these subsidies persist is due to perceived unpopularity of raising the prices of fossil fuels — even if a switch to renewables would be cheaper in the long term. You may well have seen how people react to increases in heating or petrol costs. So, for politicians to make such changes, they’d need to believe that the public is on their side. Which is actually a strange position to be in, as most people do think that climate change is a big problem.

Research and polls show that the majority of people worldwide support climate action. So why do policymakers need convincing? Well, the problem is that support on a poll doesn’t necessarily translate to action.

Madalina Vlasceanu: There is a big difference between being aware of the problem in principle and being aware of this problem viscerally at a level where you know it's affecting you personally. So we know people have an optimism bias. and even though intellectually they can conceptualize that, well, there is this problem, people are talking about it, scientists are in agreement, it is going to get worse. And we understand that. At the same time, two things can be true. And so what is also true is that people think, well, this is probably not gonna affect me, or at least not very soon. And this is the type of thing where it'll probably happen first somewhere really far away or to other people or sometime in the pretty distant future. So I'd rather spend today or the near future thinking about more immediate issues that I have to worry about.

Nick Petrić Howe: I can certainly relate to spending my time worrying about things other than climate change. So, how do you actually get people to act? Madalina’s research has revealed some clues. By testing different interventions on a sample of 30,000 US citizens, she and a team of researchers were able to see what could actually get people to collectively act on climate change.

Madalina Vlasceanu: The top intervention leveraged two processes. So the two processes are efficacy beliefs and positive emotions. So efficacy beliefs means the belief that engaging in this activity will actually pay off in the exact way in which you're hoping it will. So the belief that if I do attend this protest, this protest will then reduce the risk of climate change. And so the way in which you can achieve this efficacy belief induction is by giving people examples of times in which such participation in collective action has actually had meaningful effects.

Nick Petrić Howe: Such examples include the banning of fossil fuel extraction in Quebec due to decades of grassroots movements and Los Angeles moving to ban urban oil extraction, because of years of protests and community organising.

Madalina Vlasceanu: And the other process I mentioned is positive emotions. So in addition to feeling like you will make a difference, you also need to feel like there is an emotional benefit to you personally, not just to the cause of the participation. So meaning-making, increasing belonging, or starting some close relationships with like-minded others. All of these more personal motivations to engage in collective action are also critical to engagement.

Nick Petrić Howe: Madalina also found that appealing to ideas like preserving the purity of the environment and respect for authority can also encourage more action — and these interventions were effective across the political spectrum.

To encourage more action, these interventions could be employed by governments, NGOs, charities and people making podcasts... They could say that you can make a difference, and you may even make some friends along the way. And by encouraging people to get together and act on climate, Madalina thinks we can create a positive feedback loop where more climate action is done, which makes it easier for us all to do more climate action.

Madalina Vlasceanu: It could be, for example, that someone's very motivated to not pollute very much or not use a lot of fossil fuels, but the system doesn't necessarily facilitate these actions. So it makes it much harder for me as an individual not to pollute, even if I wanted to. And so if I participate in collective action to change some of those systemic level decisions then it could be even easier for me to engage in individual level climate action by having an easier time engaging in in individual level behavioural change, such as you know, engaging in ways of transport that are less polluting.

If you’re sceptical about the power of groups of people, then we can take lessons from historical changes of the past. During the civil rights movement in the US, collections of small groups came together and organised protests, civil disobedience and boycotts that eventually led to new civil rights laws and the end of most legal discrimation against African Americans.

Madalina Vlasceanu: the main thing an individual can do to address climate change is to be less of an individual. And so we have to recognize the power in groups in the power of our collective to making change.

Nick Petrić Howe: So, if you want to fight climate change. Remember this. You can make a change, people have done it before, and it may even be good for you to do so.

Madalina Vlasceanu: Hopelessness is pretty natural, I would say. I felt hopelessness quite a lot at the beginning of this journey when I was first becoming aware of just how big the threat is. especially when I became a mother and I understood that my kids will inherit a very different world and a much worse one. Than I had. And so hopelessness is there. the one way I found to cope or to get out of it is by taking action. So action is the antidote to hopelessness.

Nick Petrić Howe: In this podcast series, I wanted to find out if there was anything I could do about climate change. And it turns out that perhaps things are not as bad as I thought. There are certainly challenges, and some big unknowns as to what might happen in the future.

But as humans, we have a tendency to focus on the negative. And when it comes to climate change, there’s plenty of negative to think about. Even if things are not as bad as I thought, we’re not really on track to meet our climate targets. We need more action, but perhaps that’s something in which we all have a role to play.

And according to the science, we can make a difference. I’m certainly trying to. [Since starting this podcast, I’ve changed my pension to be invested in climate-conscious way, joined a group organising for climate action in my company, and started talking more to people about climate. I’m talking to you right now. And that’s helped, with my anxiety. I just hope that it helps with the world.]

In the end, I turned my climate anxiety, into what I hope is a climate superpower — I’m still anxious but I’m using that energy to push me, to try and make difference. As Madalina said, Action is the antidote to hopelessness. I hope I’ve helped you feel a bit less hopeless.

For now, I’ll leave you with a final quote from Madalina.

Nick Petrić Howe: And then my last question is: how do we save the world?

Madalina Vlasceanu: Haha, good question. In my mind how we save the world is caring about each other and helping each other out.

Nick Petrić Howe: This podcast series was written and produced by me, Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was my editor. Thanks also to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu, and, of course, my mum for talking to me for this episode. And thank you all for listening too. If you like this sort of thing, then Kimberly has got her own climate podcast, I’ll link to that in the show notes as well.

#994. Freddie Potts on the pain of leaving West Ham, why he had to move on this summer, upsetting the odds in the Champions League with Club Brugge - and why they don't fear Liverpool!

Published: 08:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 14:15 EST, 24 November 2026

There are few transfers that get West Ham supporters talking quite like the sale of an academy graduate.

Who can forget the uproar after Grady Diangana joined West Brom in 2020, when club captain Mark Noble released a public statement voicing his anger and disappointment at the move.

Noble’s thoughts were echoed by team-mates at the time, while supporters were similarly up in arms at the sale of the winger.

So, when Freddie Potts joined Club Brugge for £10million on the eve of the season to mark the controversial departure of another product of the proclaimed Academy of Football, you can imagine the reaction.

Potts represented more than a graduate. A boyhood West Ham fan whose dad Steve is a club legend and still serves as a first-team coach, he joined the academy aged six. His brother Dan also came through the ranks.

The midfielder had just enjoyed a breakthrough campaign despite West Ham’s relegation, and many felt he was the perfect player to build their Championship promotion push around.

Freddie Potts is shining in Belgium with Club Brugge after joining from West Ham in the summer

Potts joined the Hammers academy aged six and enjoyed a breakthrough year last season

Hammers favourites Kevin Nolan and Tony Cottee weighed in with their disapproval at his sale, while celebrity fan Ray Winstone expressed his shock and anger live on talkSPORT.

‘Of course you see it (the division about the move) on social media,’ Potts tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘Every player does. But even though last season was tough I always felt I had a connection with the West Ham fans.

‘No matter if I played well or bad I always felt I understood what it meant to play for West Ham. It's a great club with great fans and people. In the end, I had to do what was best for me. I wanted to play this season, and I felt like this was the best place to do that.’

Potts, 22 at the time of his exit, admits it was extremely tough and emotional for him and his family to leave a club he had been at for 16 years.

But, during pre-season he became aware he wasn’t likely to play as much as he wanted to under Nuno Espirito Santo.

‘In the end it’s the manager’s decision,’ Potts says. ‘I wasn’t getting the minutes I wanted. The feeling was that I wasn’t guaranteed to be in the plans as much as Club Brugge were promising me, so I thought it was best for me to move.

‘It was very hard. West Ham have been my club my whole life and I have a lot of love for West Ham. But I had to take into account what was best for my career and I’m loving it at Brugge. It’s a really exciting place full of great people and a great manager.’

Potts had multiple options in the summer, including Premier League interest, yet the chance to play in the Champions League and compete for titles with Brugge attracted him.

Their record of developing young players and a talented squad that includes the likes of Carlos Forbs and Nicolo Tresoldi was equally compelling, and the midfielder hasn't looked back.

Potts started Brugge’s first 10 league games, missing their final one before the international break due to suspension. He returned at the weekend as they thrashed Mechelen 5-1. Ivan Leko’s side are one point adrift of Union Saint-Gilloise at the top of the Belgian Pro League, and they have also impressed in the Champions League.

In Europe, Brugge have beaten Inter Milan, PSV and Lens on their way to nine points from 12, only narrowly losing 3-2 to Aston Villa. Potts has started each match, including their memorable 4-3 win against Inter at the San Siro, and they host Liverpool on Wednesday.

‘It's a really good group of lads,’ he says. ‘Everyone speaks English as well which helps me. It's a good team and we're happy playing with each other.’

He is clearly enjoying life and is just the fifth English player in history to play for the club. Potts did take time to settle though, and admits he initially suffered from homesickness.

‘I found it difficult because East London and Essex have been my home for my whole life,’ he says. ‘West Ham was my life. It was tough in terms of moving into a new language and everything but you get used to it and I’m really enjoying it here. It’ll be strange going back home to England.'

Potts has been a regular and has had a key role in Brugge's impressive early exploits in Europe

Brugge have beaten PSV, Lens and Inter Milan, and they take on Liverpool this Wednesday

Potts’ family have popped over to see him and he has enjoyed exploring his new surroundings. He is yet to learn the local language and scolds himself for being lazy for relying on English, although he has picked up little bits of Flemish.

He has immersed himself in the culture too, and reveals he has tried the world-famous Belgian fries and a few local beers, albeit only when he has enough time to recover between games.

Despite his new life in Europe, Potts remains a West Ham fan and tries to watch them on TV every week.

He has been surprised by their struggles on their return to the Championship for the first time in 14 years, with Nuno paying the price by losing his job. Former Hammers midfielder Scott Parker has since taken the reins.

‘I still think they're playing well,’ Potts says. ‘They've got a great team and Scott Parker is a really good manager. You get ups and downs but I still 100 per cent think West Ham will get promoted this year.'

Potts’ stay in the Hammers first team may have been brief, yet there were still plenty of highs, not least a storming performance on his first Premier League start. That came in a win over Newcastle last November in the Hammers’ first home victory of the season. He was also coached by his dad, an experience he jokes had positives and negatives.

He left West Ham after realising he was unlikely to be first choice under Nuno Espirito Santo

Potts is a boyhood West Ham fan and is fully expecting them to get promoted this season

Attention now turns to Brugge’s clash against Liverpool. It promises to be a tricky challenge for Andoni Iraola’s side against a team who are determined to prove themselves on the European stage.

The two teams are level on points in the league phase, and Potts is keen for his side to take another scalp.

‘I don't think there's much difference in the way we've been performing in the Champions League,’ Potts concludes. ‘It'll be difficult for them to come to our place as well.

‘They're a great team, but we're going to approach it like we have with every Champions League game. We've gone away and beaten Milan, we've beaten PSV away. These are top teams.

‘Results like that give you a boost of how far you can go. You don't want to look too far ahead but every game in this competition is a chance to show everyone what you can do.

‘Liverpool will be a tough game but we've proved it against top teams before and we're going in thinking that we can do it again.’

#991. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League group stage match between RB Leipzig and Manchester City from Saxony. The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

The Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

These two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

#983. Germany hopes to host world ice hockey championship — without Russia

International protests continue after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey. Germany is seeking a solution that will allow the country to host next year's world championship.

A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

Kornelius said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.
